title: Higher yields: a benign mix for equities, for now - Barclays Private Bank
text: Barclays Home Contact us Log in Menu Higher yields: a benign mix for equities, for now 2 October 2026 Dorothée Deck, Head of Cross Asset Strategy Share this Insight Share page via Facebook Share page via X Share page via LinkedIn Share page via email This article is technical in nature and may require some background knowledge and experience in investing to understand the themes that we explore below. All data referenced in this article is sourced from Bloomberg unless otherwise stated, and is accurate at the time of publishing. Summary US 10-year yields have risen by 130 basis points since the end of February, to 5.24% at the time of writing. Higher yields usually favour cheaper, shorter-duration stocks over growth, yet the opposite has happened at the index level: Value has underperformed Growth by around 3%. The composition of a yield move matters more for equities than its level. Close to four fifths of this one reflects higher expected real short-term interest rates, which we read largely as a repricing of the US Federal Reserve's policy path on resilient growth and sticky inflation. That mix has been comparatively benign for companies with strong, visible earnings. Beneath the surface, the expected rotation has taken place. Value's underperformance at the index level reflects its sector mix, notably its underweight in technology, while within sectors cheaper stocks have outperformed. Valuation discipline has therefore been rewarded at the stock level rather than through style allocation. The remaining fifth, from the term premium and inflation expectations, is where we would focus attention. The main risks are a shift in the mix towards those components, particularly through energy-driven inflation, or slower growth undermining the earnings offset. Yields are high, but the market has not behaved as expected The US 10-year yield now sits at around 5.2% at the time of writing, a level last seen in 2007, with the 30-year above 5.6%. Conventional thinking would suggest this should be uncomfortable for equity valuations, and uncomfortable in a fairly specific way: higher discount rates weigh most heavily on companies whose value rests on cash flows far into the future, which would normally favour cheaper, shorter-duration parts of the market. That is not what has happened. Since the end of February, MSCI World Value has underperformed Growth by around 3%. Within the MSCI World index over the same period, Information Technology gained 34%, compared with 8% for the index as a whole, while utilities fell 14% and consumer staples and real estate around 10%. Market leadership has, if anything, moved further towards growth, and technology in particular. It is tempting to read this as markets ignoring the bond market. We think a closer look at where the yield move has come from offers a more straightforward explanation. Where the move has come from Not all increases in yields carry the same message. A useful way to think about the current move is to separate it into three components. The term premium cannot be observed directly, so we rely on a widely used estimate from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Breakeven inflation, by contrast, can be read directly from bond prices. What is left once those two are taken out is a residual, which mainly captures the change in expected real short-term interest rates over the next ten years. This residual is the largest component by some distance, accounting for around 100 basis points (bp), or around 78% of the total move. We read it largely as a repricing of the US Federal Reserve's (Fed) policy path. Short-rate expectations have swung sharply: December 2026 SOFR futures now imply a rate of around 4.3%, up from 3.1% at the end of February, as markets moved from pricing cuts to pricing hikes. Because the residual is derived from the other two components, it inherits any error in them and should be read as an approximation. Markets are pricing a more hawkish Fed because activity has held up and inflation has proved persistent, not because its credibility is in question. The limited rise in breakevens supports that reading. The second component is the term premium, the additional compensation investors require for holding longer-dated bonds rather than rolling short-term bills. This has risen by around 20bp, or 15% of the move. The third is inflation expectations, with 10-year breakevens up around 9 basis points, or 7%. Together, the latter two represent roughly a fifth of the increase. This is the part more likely to reflect unease about the fiscal path and about supply-driven inflation rather than about economic strength. Higher expected real short-term rates account for most of the rise in yields Contributions to the change in the US 10-year Treasury yield between 27 February and 29 September 2026 Source: Bloomberg, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Barclays Private Bank, September 2026 Note: We decompose the change in the US 10-year Treasury yield since 27 February 2026 into three components: the change in 10-year breakeven inflation, the change in the Adrian, Crump and Moench (ACM) 10-year term premium estimated by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and a residual. The residual is the change in the yield less the other two components, so the three sum to the total by construction. We interpret it as the change in expected real short-term interest rates over the next ten years. It also absorbs overlaps between breakevens and the term premium (both contain an inflation risk premium), TIPS liquidity effects and model estimation error, and should be read as an approximation. What could make this less benign We would watch three developments in particular. The term premium could reprice higher. It has already been higher this year, peaking at around 0.89% in mid-August and falling back close to its February level by late September. It then rose by around 20bp in the last week of September, accounting for most of that week's rise in yields. The market is clearly sensitive to the issue rather than settled on it. With the deficit above 6% of gross domestic product (GDP), gross debt of around $40 trillion and reduced participation from price-insensitive official and foreign buyers, the November Quarterly Refunding and the long-dated auctions that follow will show how readily the market is absorbing supply. Weak demand at the long end would lift the term premium, and that is a component that raises the discount rate without improving the earnings outlook. Inflation expectations have been volatile and could inflect higher. Breakevens reached 2.52% in early May before falling to 2.19% in late June and recovering to around 2.35%. With the price of Brent above $103 a barrel and tensions around the Strait of Hormuz unresolved, further energy price pressure would push breakevens higher for supply-side reasons. That form of inflation squeezes real incomes and margins rather than signalling demand strength, and it complicates the Fed's position. Growth may also slow. The hawkish repricing assumes that activity stays resilient, but tighter financial conditions tend to feed through to the real economy over time. Early signs are emerging on both sides of the Atlantic. Eurozone business lending halved in August, while in the US, mortgage rates have moved back above 7% and mortgage applications are down by more than a third from a year ago. The third-quarter reporting season, which begins with the US banks in mid-October and includes the large technology companies at the end of the month, will be an important test of whether earnings are holding up in line with the market's assumption. Why the composition matters for equity leadership Work on the relationship between bond yields and equities suggests that several factors determine how damaging a rise in yields proves to be. The level of yields is one: historically, 10-year yields around 5% or real yields above 2.5% have been more challenging. Both thresholds have now been crossed, with the 10-year real yield at around 2.9%. The speed of adjustment is another, with gradual moves easier to absorb than abrupt ones. The point in the cycle matters too. But the most relevant here is the source of the move. Where yields rise because growth and inflation are running hotter than expected, nominal earnings tend to rise alongside the discount rate, and the two effects partially offset. Where yields rise because investors demand more compensation for fiscal risk, or because energy prices are pushing up costs, there is no equivalent offset. Since the end of February, the move has been predominantly of the first kind. That helps explain why companies with strong, visible and near-term earnings have been able to absorb a materially higher discount rate, and why the expected rotation towards cheaper, shorter-duration stocks has not materialised at the index level. Equity leadership has not followed the rise in bond yields Six-month change in MSCI World Value relative to Growth (%) and in the US 10-year Treasury yield Source: LSEG Datastream, Barclays Private Bank, September 2026 The rotation is happening, but beneath the surface Looking underneath the style indices offers a further observation. Value's underperformance since the end of February is more than fully explained by sector allocation, principally its substantial underweight in information technology relative to Growth, alongside overweights in utilities and consumer staples. Both of those sectors fell in absolute terms as yields rose, behaving as the bond proxies they are rather than as defensive ballast. Stock selection tells a different story. Within sectors, cheaper companies have generally outperformed more expensive ones, including within technology itself. This is consistent with what a higher discount rate would be expected to produce and it has been obscured at the index level by the scale of technology's sector return. For portfolios built from the bottom up, this seems to us the more relevant observation. Valuation discipline has been rewarded over the period, but at the stock level rather than through style allocation. Where the vulnerabilities sit The principal vulnerability is therefore a shift in the composition of the yield move towards the term premium or energy-driven inflation, which would raise the discount rate without the earnings offset that has cushioned equities so far. Market concentration amplifies this. The S&P 500 remains within roughly 1% of its record high, while the median constituent trades around 16% below its own 52-week high, the widest gap since the dot-com era. A market carried by a narrow group of companies has limited capacity to absorb a rotation should leadership stall. Market breadth is at its narrowest since the dot-com era The gap between the S&P 500 and its median constituent's distance from 52-week highs, measured in percentage points, with long-term average and ±1 standard deviation Sources: LSEG Datastream, Barclays Private Bank, September 2026 Implications for equity investors Three implications follow, in our view. First, not all quality growth companies are equally exposed to higher yields. Those with high returns on capital, pricing power and good near-term earnings visibility have coped well so far. Those whose valuations rely on profits many years ahead would be more vulnerable to a further rise in the term premium. We find this distinction more helpful than the growth and value labels Second, we would be cautious about treating traditional bond proxies as defensive at these yield levels. Utilities, real estate and consumer staples have all fallen meaningfully since the end of February, and rotating into them as a risk-reduction measure would not have achieved that objective Third, given the degree of concentration, diversification within growth exposure looks prudent. That means spreading exposure across the technology value chain and favouring companies able to demonstrate monetisation and capital discipline, rather than holding concentrated positions in the most crowded names. We remain invested and constructive, but increasingly selective. Our preferences are now limited to a narrow set of sectors (technology and energy) and geographies (emerging markets), having recently neutralised our constructive view on healthcare and negative view on communication services. This reflects our view that most of the opportunity lies at the stock level. In this context, the upcoming earnings season will be an important test as to whether the market can remain supported by its current leadership or whether some reshuffling (and therefore potential short-term downside risk) is required.
